newsitem.title: USA: Mich. boom eased tax reform fallout - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Mich. boom eased tax reform fallout - Moody's.

text.p: Michigan's "extraordinary economic boom" has eased the potential financial problems that could have arisen as a result of the state's tax reform measures passed in 1995, Moody's Investors Service reported in its Credit Perspectives publication on Friday.

The Michigan boom has resulted in increased enrollments for public schools that partially offset increased expenditures and has masked, at least for now, the problems associated with tax caps for the municipalities, Moody's said.

"Administrators who are able to recognize and adapt to the changing revenue criteria under the new system should be able to maintain or improve their credit quality, even under the limitations imposed by Proposal A," Moody's said.
Michigan voters approved increases in sales and cigarette taxes, the real estate transfer tax and a statewide property tax levy in 1995 while eliminating the use of most local property taxes.

There have been no significant credit quality changes as a result of the tax reforms, but Moody's outlook remains cautious while schools and municipalities develop strategies to cope with it, Moody's said.
Credit strength for school districts now rests with a school district's ability to maintain or increase enrollment, Moody's said.

The state school aid formula limits excessive growth or decline in revenue for most districts, while also guaranteeing a base level of funding, Moody's said. The growth in the foundation allowance for all but the poorest districts remains at 2 percent to 3 percent and smaller increases in less economically successful periods remains a concern, Moody's said.

"For Michigan's counties, cities and townships -- which are typically property tax-dependent and already face strict tax rate limits -- the amendment specified under Proposal A represents a potential long-term credit negative," Moody's said.

In an economic slowdown, the economic restrictions in the tax reform plan "will become more relevant," with the restrictions less important to municipalities with strong growth potential, Moody's said.
"Moody's finds that cities that levy an income tax are significantly less bulernable to Proposal A's property tax growth limitations," the publication reported.
